To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please talk to your kids about the blue pills

I’m posting this as a new message because the police warning on the noticeboard deserves to be seen, and the rumours in the Saturday thread aren’t helping anyone. Please don’t guess about what happened or who was involved.

Police are warning that blue tablets sold as diazepam or Xanax may contain nitazenes — synthetic opioids that can be much stronger than heroin. If someone who’s taken something becomes extremely drowsy, has pinpoint pupils, slow or noisy breathing, or blue lips, call 999 straight away. Don’t put them to bed to sleep it off, and don’t wait to see if they improve. With opioid poisoning, breathing can slow or stop, leaving the brain without oxygen. Time matters.

I know people panic. They may think the person just needs to sleep, or worry they’ll get themselves or their mate in trouble. But please call for help immediately. The police have said their priority is preserving life. If someone is unwell, getting them urgent help matters most.

Naloxone nasal spray can reverse an opioid overdose. Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, provides free kits to anyone who asks — no names needed. The training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10–4, and until 7 on Thursdays.

And please, let’s stop slagging kids off. It doesn’t protect anyone. If teenagers think they’ll be blamed or punished, they may be too scared to ring for help when someone is in danger. They need to know they can call 999 and that adults will help.

I had the chat with my 14-year-old over tea last night. There were a few eye rolls, but he listened and asked what pinpoint pupils meant. It doesn’t have to be a perfect conversation. Please talk to your kids this week — not after half term, not “when there’s a good moment”. Tell them what the warning signs are, to call 999, and not to leave someone to sleep it off.

Please share this post so it reaches parents and teenagers who might not see the police warning. A share could help someone get help in time.
